nameStory: The Curlew Sandpiper gets its name from its distinctive curved bill that resembles a miniature version of the much larger curlew's famous downward-curving beak. This graceful curve helps it probe deeper into sand and mud than straight-billed sandpipers can reach. The name perfectly captures this bird's most distinctive feature in a way that helps birdwatchers remember it.
description: The Curlew Sandpiper is a small, elegant shorebird that's quite rare in New England - a true prize for birdwatchers with only about 30 recorded sightings in the region. This long-distance traveler normally breeds in Arctic Siberia and winters in Africa, making any New England appearance a special vagrant occurrence. It's a medium-sized sandpiper with a gracefully curved bill and striking seasonal plumage changes, from rusty-red breeding colors to subtle gray-brown winter tones.

idTips.label: Curved Bill
idTips.description: The bill curves gently downward like a miniature curlew's, longer and more curved than most other sandpipers - you can see this distinctive banana-like shape even from a distance

idTips.label: White Rump Patch
idTips.description: In flight, shows a bright white rump that contrasts sharply with the darker back and wings - this white patch is more extensive than in most similar sandpipers

idTips.label: Breeding Plumage
idTips.description: In spring and early summer, the entire head, neck, and chest turn a rich rusty-red color that's deeper and more extensive than similar species

idTips.label: Juvenile Feathers
idTips.description: Young birds have a distinctive peachy-buff wash on the breast and wing feathers with pale edges that create a neat, scaly pattern

idTips.label: Feeding Behavior
idTips.description: Uses that curved bill to probe deeply into sand and mud with methodical, purposeful jabs rather than the rapid pecking of straight-billed sandpipers

habitat: Look for Curlew Sandpipers on mudflats, sandy beaches, and shallow tidal pools along the coast during migration periods. They prefer areas with soft substrate where they can probe deeply with their curved bills. Since they're vagrants to New England, they're most often found mixed in with flocks of other sandpipers at prime shorebird locations like Plum Island or Cape Cod.

seasonality.spring: Extremely rare vagrant during spring migration (April-May), when any individuals would likely be in their striking rusty-red breeding plumage.
seasonality.summer: Occasional vagrant sightings possible in late summer (July-August) when birds might appear in worn breeding plumage or beginning molt.
seasonality.fall: Best chance for sightings during fall migration (August-October), when birds appear in gray-brown non-breeding plumage or distinctive peachy juvenile plumage.
seasonality.winter: Not expected in New England winters as this species migrates to tropical regions in Africa, Asia, and Australia.

funFact: Male Curlew Sandpipers perform an elaborate courtship ritual where they build fake nests in the ground just to show off to females - like a bird version of building a model home to impress a potential mate!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with Dunlin, but the Curlew Sandpiper's bill curves down throughout its length while a Dunlin's bill only droops at the very tip. Remember: Curlew = Curved throughout, Dunlin = Droopy tip only.
contextualKnowledge: This species is a true vagrant in New England - meaning it's far outside its normal range when seen here. Every sighting is noteworthy and should be reported to eBird, as these rare visitors help scientists understand changing migration patterns and climate impacts.
compareHints: Among its Calidris sandpiper relatives, the Curlew Sandpiper's curved bill immediately sets it apart from straight-billed species like Sanderling and Semipalmated Sandpiper. It's larger than the small 'peeps' like Least Sandpiper but smaller than Red Knot, with a much more pronounced bill curve than the slightly droopy-tipped Dunlin.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the Calidris sandpipers, sanderlings are notably stockier with a thicker bill than the needle-billed Least Sandpiper or Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Within the Calidris genus, Semipalmated Sandpipers are most similar to Western Sandpipers but have blunter, shorter bills and less rusty coloring in breeding plumage.
Among its Calidris cousins, the Least Sandpiper's yellow-green legs immediately set it apart from the black-legged Semipalmated and Sanderling.

Among the Calidris sandpipers, dunlin are larger than the "peeps" (semipalmated, least, and white-rumped sandpipers) but smaller than red knot, with that diagnostic curved bill that none of the others possess.
Among the many Calidris sandpipers, Purple Sandpiper is unique for its consistently dark plumage and exclusive rocky habitat preference.
Among the Calidris sandpipers, White-rumped is most similar to Baird's Sandpiper, but Baird's lacks the white rump and has a more buff-colored breast.

Among the Calidris sandpipers in New England, pectoral sandpipers are distinguished by their larger size and that signature sharp breast line - dunlin have curved bills and different streaking, while the various 'peeps' (least, semipalmated) are much smaller.
Among the Calidris sandpipers, Red Knot is the second-largest and most robust, much chunkier than Sanderling or Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Among New England's Calidris sandpipers, the Stilt Sandpiper is the tallest and longest-legged, easily distinguished from the tiny 'peeps' like Least and Semipalmated Sandpipers.
Among the small Calidris sandpipers, Baird's stands out with its notably long wing projection past the tail - much longer than Semipalmated or Least Sandpipers.
Among New England's Calidris sandpipers, Buff-breasted is unique for its solid peachy-tan underparts and preference for grassy areas over mudflats.

Among New England's small sandpipers, Western Sandpipers are most easily confused with Semipalmated Sandpipers, but Westerns have longer, more drooped bill tips and often show more rusty coloring in breeding plumage.
Among Calidris sandpipers, Ruffs are unique in their extreme sexual size difference - much more pronounced than in Dunlin or Pectoral Sandpipers.
Among its Calidris relatives in New England, Little Stint is smaller than Least Sandpiper (already our tiniest regular sandpiper) and much smaller than Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Compared to other small Calidris sandpipers in New England, Red-necked Stint is smaller than Semipalmated Sandpiper and has darker legs than Least Sandpiper.
Among the Calidris sandpipers, Sharp-tailed is most similar to Pectoral Sandpiper in size and habitat preferences, but lacks the Pectoral's sharply cut breast band.
Among Calidris sandpipers, the Surfbird is uniquely stocky and rock-adapted, unlike its beach and mudflat-loving relatives.
